extracted.intended_audience: educated readers, literary critics, poets, playwrights, actors, and polite society interested in poetry, theatre, and manners
extracted.subtask_description: Practical literary-critical guidance on composing and judging heroic/epic poetry and theatrical performance, plus social methods for correcting conversational vices and cultivating character. Emphasis on Milton, stagecraft, and moral effects of art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Epic should end happily
rubrics_metrics.description: An Heroick Poem, according to the opinion of the best Criticks, ought to end happily, and leave the Mind of the Reader, after having conducted it through many Doubts and Fears, Sorrows and Disquietudes, in a State of Tranquility and Satisfaction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the principal fable lacks an inherently happy ending, the poet should find a method to supply this defect (e.g., represent the Adversary defeated and the protagonists comforted). Scoring note: the poem's resolution should restore the reader's peace and moral satisfaction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fable (plot/coherent subject)
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate the poem's fable—the main story idea and its suitability as the foundation of a heroic poem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The fable should support heroic scope and moral deductions; even if not explicitly chosen before composition, a just heroick poem should allow derivation of a great moral. Ensure episodes serve the main fable (e.g., Milton confines an episode to the line of Abraham to give focus).

rubrics_metrics.name: Characters (delineation and moral function)
rubrics_metrics.description: Characters should be distinct, appropriate to their roles, and serve the moral and emotional movement of the poem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Villainy and heroism must be convincingly represented (e.g., Satan rendered miserable at his height of triumph; Adam shown triumphant even amid misery). Characters can illustrate under-morals; judge by the consistency of their actions with the poem's moral.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sentiments (moral and emotional tone)
rubrics_metrics.description: The sentiments expressed in the poem should be moral, instructive, and produce appropriate emotional responses in the reader.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sentiments must uplift or instruct (e.g., last speeches full of moral and instructive sentiments). Assess whether passages produce rapture, consolation, or proper moral reflection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Language (expression, diction, and style)
rubrics_metrics.description: The language of an heroick poem must be apt—sometimes sublime, sometimes soft, sometimes natural—and fitted to occasion and passion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge passages by whether they are sublime, soft, or natural and whether expression suits passion or moral purpose. Assess poetic diction, strength of description, and appropriateness of allusion and imitation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance religious/divine focus with poetic quality
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid attending so exclusively to Divinity or theological correctness that poetic qualities are neglected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Narration should sustain poetic rise and ornament where appropriate; watch for places where doctrinal attention makes the poem flag. Example anti-pattern: passages that are theologically precise but poetically inert.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use poetical ornaments where subject allows
rubrics_metrics.description: Employ poetical ornaments (vivid imagery, dramatised confusion, powerful natural descriptions) in episodes that admit them, e.g., Babel, Plagues of Egypt, storms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use descriptive strength in scenes capable of poetical decoration; evaluate descriptive energy (e.g., 'Storm of Hail and Fire... described with great Strength').

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate use of scriptural allusion
rubrics_metrics.description: Scripture may be a source of noble images and allusions; borrowing from scripture is acceptable when it serves poetic elevation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allusion should be transformed into poetic image (e.g., 'River-Dragon' from Ezekiel). Copying should be judicious—retain poetical force rather than literal citation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judicious classical imitation
rubrics_metrics.description: Imitate classical authors (Virgil, Homer, Tasso) where it improves the poem; imitation should be judicious and used to raise one’s own imagination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Imitation must be adapted, not slavishly copied; use hints from classical visions (e.g., Virgil’s Æneid) to enrich episodes and names, but prioritize original poetic invention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Episode focus and selection
rubrics_metrics.description: Select and confine episodes to material that advances the poem's purpose and gives particular liveliness (e.g., focusing on Abraham’s line when illustrating Messiah).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Episodes should have a clear relation to the main fable and contribute to reader engagement; evaluate for relevance and vividness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representation of emotional arcs
rubrics_metrics.description: Depict the protagonists' emotional development (joy, hope, consolation) convincingly so the reader experiences parallel consolation or transport.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scenes of revelation or promise (e.g., Adam rejoicing at visions of the Messiah) should be rendered to provoke corresponding reader emotion; assess intensity and authenticity of feeling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral unity and instructiveness
rubrics_metrics.description: An heroick poem should embody a universal and useful moral (the 'soul of the fable') and also afford many under-morals in its parts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether a clear central moral can be deduced (e.g., 'Obedience to the Will of God makes Men happy...') and whether smaller episodes yield instructive lessons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Structural organization (division and disposition)
rubrics_metrics.description: Organize the work into parts (books) with just and regular disposition; divisions should aid comprehension and flow rather than mimicry for its own sake.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether book divisions are made for clarity and regularity (Milton’s revision from ten to twelve books praised for judgment). Avoid arbitrary division merely to resemble classics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Temporal coherence of action
rubrics_metrics.description: Maintain a coherent timeline for actions occurring within natural regions; where action is within nature, time should be calculable and sensible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check consistency of days/months in the action (example: Milton’s action from Adam’s appearance to expulsion spans ten days). Supernatural regions may be exempt from temporal calculations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Taxonomy of poetic beauties
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize different causes of beauty: sublime, soft, natural; beauties recommended by passion, moral, sentiment, or expression.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When judging passages, classify why they are beautiful (invention, allusion, imitation, expression) to give precise critical praise or censure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Genius shown by invention and allusion
rubrics_metrics.description: The poet’s genius appears through happy invention, distant allusion, and judicious imitation rather than mere borrowing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Value originality in images and the skillful integration of allusion; prefer imaginative elevation over mere citation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stage's social influence (moral responsibility of theatre)
rubrics_metrics.description: Because the stage transfuses manners and customs to the world, evaluate performances by what passions/sentiments they encourage or cultivate in society.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess plays for their public moral effect; support judicious encouragement of the stage when performances elevate manners, or suppression if corrupting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accurate portrayal of character-traits in acting
rubrics_metrics.description: Actors should convincingly represent specific traits (tenderness, contrition, winning emptiness, officiousness, petulancy) so audiences learn to detest or admire accordingly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge actors by fidelity to character (examples: Wilks’ tenderness, Cibber’s false pretensions, Johnson’s Corbacchio producing detestation of avarice). Good imitation can reform public taste.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comedy as a corrective device
rubrics_metrics.description: Well-regulated comic characters can put vices, follies, and social absurdities 'out of countenance' and thereby improve public manners.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourage comic representation that exposes and shames vice rather than merely ridiculing individuals. Evaluate whether comedy promotes reform and refinement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dancing, gesture, and motion as dramatic tools
rubrics_metrics.description: Gesture, motion, and dancing enhance character representation—actors should be taught suitable movement to express modesty, confidence, joy, impatience, solicitude, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess physical performance: graceful, varied gestures and purposeful movement (sliding, gliding, expressive steps) increase theatrical and moral effect; teaching dance is recommended to polish performances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ethical use of ridicule and jest
rubrics_metrics.description: Jests and burlesque entertainments without moral purpose are to be discouraged; ridicule should not be practiced merely for hurt or pastime.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish reparative or corrective humour (used to reform habits) from malicious practical jokes (packing stammerers, oglers) that humiliate. Anti-pattern: jokes that provoke anger or duels.

rubrics_metrics.name: Social-correction method: gathering to expose shared vice
rubrics_metrics.description: A social method to reform conversational vices is to assemble people who display the same fault so they become self-aware and correct it (e.g., grouping those who overuse expletives, swear, or tell long stories).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use gentle exposure (e.g., private amanuensis taking notes and reading them) to prompt self-reflection; ensure moderation to avoid resentment—monitor for backfire (some guests may take offense).

rubrics_metrics.name: Modesty (definition and signs)
rubrics_metrics.description: Modesty is the reflection of an ingenuous mind, felt as self-censure when one has committed or imagines committing an action worthy of censure; a truly modest person blushes even when alone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate modesty by internal conscience and consistent behavior alone and in company; exemplary instances move others more than eloquence (example: the prince who was overpowered by modesty).

rubrics_metrics.name: Assurance (definition and foundations)
rubrics_metrics.description: Assurance is the faculty of possessing one’s self—saying and doing indifferent things without uneasiness—rooted in moderate knowledge of the world and a mind fixed to do nothing against honour and decency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess assurance by steadiness under misinterpretation and ability to despise small censures due to conscious integrity. Distinguish assurance from impudence: true assurance rests on principle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cultivate both modesty and assurance
rubrics_metrics.description: Both modesty and assurance are desirable and complementary: modesty prevents loss of honour and virtue; assurance prevents being made uneasy by others’ folly or ill-nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourage practices that develop reflection and self-possession in equal measure; note consequences when either is lacking (uneasiness or loss of honour).
